title: Jellyfish & Stingray Stings in Cabo: What to Do
description: Stung by a jellyfish or stingray at a Cabo beach? First aid, when to call 911 and how to get a doctor to your hotel for $189 USD, tax included, 24/7.
h1: Jellyfish and stingray stings at Cabo beaches: what to do

intro: Snorkeling at a calm cove, wading at a sandy beach, paddleboarding along the coast: the Sea of Cortez is one of the best parts of a Los Cabos vacation. Once in a while, though, the ocean pushes back with a sting from a jellyfish or a stingray. Most stings are painful but manageable, and knowing what to do in the first few minutes makes a real difference.

Call 911 right away if the person has trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, chest pain, fainting, confusion or a sting to the chest, neck or abdomen. For everything else, this guide covers first aid, what to avoid and how to get an English-speaking doctor to your hotel, villa or yacht.

sections.h2: Emergency first: when a sting needs 911
p: Get emergency help immediately, and get the person out of the water safely first, if any of these happen after a sting:
list: Difficulty breathing, wheezing, a tight throat or trouble swallowing
Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat, or hives spreading over the body
Chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, fainting or confusion
Severe muscle cramps, vomiting or weakness that keeps getting worse
A stingray barb that has entered the chest, neck or abdomen, or a deep wound with heavy bleeding
A large area of stings on a small child, an older adult or someone with heart or lung disease
p_after: If the person has a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector for allergies, use it as their doctor instructed and still call 911. Do not try to pull out a barb that is lodged deep in the body; keep the person still and let emergency staff handle it.
Severe allergic reactions can happen with marine stings too. Our guide to allergic reactions and hives in Cabo explains the warning signs in more detail.

sections.h2: Jellyfish stings: first aid on the beach
p: Jellyfish tentacles carry thousands of tiny stinging cells. Contact usually causes instant burning pain, red lines or welts that follow the shape of the tentacle, itching and sometimes swelling. Here is what generally helps:
list: Get out of the water calmly, so you do not brush against more tentacles.
Rinse the area with seawater, not fresh water. Fresh water can make remaining stinging cells fire.
Remove any visible tentacles with tweezers, the edge of a card or a gloved hand. Do not touch them with bare fingers.
Do not rub the skin with sand or a towel, and skip folk remedies like urine, alcohol or meat tenderizer.
Follow the advice of local lifeguards. Recommended rinses differ depending on the type of jellyfish, and what works for one species can be useless for another.
Once the tentacles are off, soaking the area in hot water (as hot as is comfortable, never scalding) often eases the pain. A cold pack is an alternative if hot water is not available.
p_after: Pain usually starts to settle within hours, while redness and itching may last a few days. Some people develop a delayed itchy rash at the same spot a week or two later. Ask a doctor or pharmacist before using any cream or medicine, especially for children, during pregnancy or if you take other medications.

sections.h2: Stingray stings: why hot water matters
p: Stingrays like to rest half-buried in warm, shallow, sandy water. They are not aggressive, but if you step on one, the tail can whip up and leave a puncture or cut, usually on the foot or ankle. The pain is often intense, comes on right away and can spread up the leg.
First aid for a stingray sting:
list: Leave the water and sit or lie down. Keep the leg still.
Control any bleeding with gentle, direct pressure using a clean cloth.

Soak the wound in hot water, as hot as the person can comfortably tolerate without burning. Test the temperature with an unaffected hand first, since intense pain can hide a burn. Many people find this the single most helpful step.
Rinse out sand and visible debris. Do not dig deep into the wound.
Do not apply ice, which tends to make this kind of pain worse.
p_after: Every stingray wound should be checked by a doctor, even when the pain improves. Small pieces of the barb or sheath can stay in the wound, and puncture wounds from the ocean have a real risk of infection. A doctor can clean the wound properly, check whether imaging is needed and review your tetanus status.

sections.h2: Other things that sting or bite in the water
p: Jellyfish and stingrays get the most attention, but a few other sea creatures can cause trouble for swimmers and snorkelers:
list: Sea urchins. Stepping on one can leave brittle spines in the skin. Do not dig for spines that are deep; a doctor can assess them.
Coral and rocks. Coral cuts look minor but are prone to infection. Clean them well and watch them over the next days.
Fish with venomous spines. Some reef fish can sting when handled. First aid is similar to a stingray: hot water and a medical check.
Tiny larvae and stinging plankton. These can cause an itchy rash under a swimsuit. Remove the swimsuit, shower and wash the suit before wearing it again.

sections.h2: When to see a doctor in Cabo
p: Even without emergency signs, arrange a medical visit if:
list: You were stung by a stingray, or there may be a spine or fragment in the skin
The pain is severe or not easing after a few hours
The sting covers a large area of skin, or it is on the face, eyes or genitals
A child, a pregnant traveler or someone with a heart condition or diabetes was stung
In the following days the area becomes warmer, more swollen, red streaks appear, there is pus or you develop a fever
You are not sure when you last had a tetanus shot
p_after: Infection is a bigger risk than many people expect with ocean wounds, so keep an eye on the area for several days and do not wait if it is getting worse instead of better.

sections.h2: How to lower your risk at the beach
p: A few simple habits keep most stings from happening in the first place:
list: Check beach flags and ask lifeguards or your hotel about jellyfish before swimming.
Do the stingray shuffle: slide your feet along the sand in shallow water instead of stepping, so rays sense you and swim away.
Wear water shoes on sandy and rocky beaches, and a rash guard or thin wetsuit for long snorkel sessions.
Do not touch marine life, coral or anything washed up on the sand, even if it looks dead.
Swim at beaches that are known to be safe for swimming, and never swim alone or after drinking alcohol.
Pack a small kit with tweezers, a clean cloth and a sealed bottle of drinking water in your beach bag.

faq.q: Should I pour fresh water or vinegar on a jellyfish sting?
faq.a: Rinse with seawater, not fresh water, which can make remaining stinging cells fire. Whether vinegar helps depends on the type of jellyfish, so follow local lifeguard advice. Remove tentacles without bare hands and see a doctor if pain is severe.

faq.q: Do I need a doctor for a stingray sting?
faq.a: Yes. Soak the wound in hot water you can comfortably tolerate as first aid, but every stingray wound should be checked, since pieces of the barb can remain and ocean wounds can get infected. Call 911 for a sting to the chest, neck or abdomen.

faq.q: Can a doctor come to my hotel for a sting in Cabo?
faq.a: Yes. A house call costs $189 USD, tax included, and requests are taken 24/7 in English and Spanish; the arrival time is confirmed when you book. For trouble breathing, swelling of the throat or fainting, call 911 instead.

faq.q: Are there jellyfish in Cabo San Lucas?
faq.a: Jellyfish can appear in the waters around Los Cabos, and conditions change with the season and currents. Ask lifeguards or your hotel before swimming and watch for posted warnings or flags at the beach.
